# Lesson 5: 2016 to 2021, Yield Curve Control and the Long Grind

*How the BOJ stopped promising a quantity of bond buying and started promising a price, why a labour market tighter than any in forty years still did not lift prices, and how the central bank ended up owning half the government bond market.*

---

## What was pressing

How to keep monetary policy stimulative for years, perhaps decades, without wrecking the banking system or running out of bonds to buy. The BOJ had learned that more of the same was no longer working. It needed a framework it could sustain for the long haul.

---

## From quantity to price

In September 2016, after a "comprehensive assessment" of its own policies, the BOJ introduced **QQE with yield curve control (YCC)**. It kept the short-term rate at −0.1% and added something no major central bank had tried since the US Federal Reserve capped Treasury yields in the 1940s: a target for the **10-year government bond yield**, set at "around zero percent".

Instead of promising to buy a fixed quantity of bonds, the BOJ now promised to buy *whatever quantity was needed* to hold the yield in place. Its ultimate weapon was the **fixed-rate purchase operation**: an offer to buy unlimited amounts of a bond at a set yield. If the market price of a 10-year bond fell so far that its yield rose above the cap, the BOJ would stand there buying until it came back.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 360" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Line chart of the 10-year Japanese government bond yield, daily, 2016 to mid-2024, with the band the Bank of Japan allowed under yield curve control. The yield fell to about minus 0.3% in July 2016. After yield curve control began in September 2016 it was pinned close to zero, within about 0.1 percentage point either side, then within 0.2 from July 2018 and 0.25 from March 2021. In 2022, as global yields rose, it pressed against the 0.25% ceiling until the band was widened to 0.5% in December 2022. In 2023 the cap was loosened to 1%, first as a hard limit and then as a reference, and yield curve control was abandoned in March 2024." fill="none" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

### The logic was clever

- **It let the yield curve breathe.** Pinning the 10-year yield near zero, rather than pushing it ever lower, allowed longer-term yields to rise a little. That eased the pressure on banks, insurers and pension funds, which earn their living from the gap between short and long rates.
- **Credibility did the work.** Because markets believed the BOJ would defend its target, it did not actually need to buy as much. By 2019 its net purchases had fallen far below the ¥80 trillion annual pace that officially remained its guideline. Analysts called it **"stealth tapering"**.
- **It promised to overshoot.** The BOJ pledged to keep expanding the money supply until inflation *exceeded* 2% and stayed above it in a stable manner. This **overshooting commitment** was meant to convince the public that it would not repeat the early exits of 2000 and 2006.

The band was not fixed for ever. It was quietly understood to be about 0.1 percentage point either side of zero at first, widened to 0.2 in July 2018 and set formally at 0.25 in March 2021. The chart shows what happened next, in Lesson 6: in 2022 the yield pressed against its ceiling until the BOJ gave way.

---

## A tight labour market, but stubborn prices

The economy settled into steady, unspectacular growth. Unemployment fell to around 2.2% to 2.4% by 2019, and the ratio of job openings to applicants reached its highest since the early 1970s. In a textbook economy that would have pushed wages and prices sharply higher. In Japan, core inflation hovered between about 0.5% and 1%.

The relationship economists call the **Phillips curve**, which says that low unemployment pushes up wages and prices, looked almost flat. Economists point to several reasons, and they reinforced each other.

1. **Expectations were anchored at zero.** Firms feared that raising prices would drive customers to rivals, so nobody moved first.
2. **Labour supply kept expanding.** Women and older people entered work in large numbers, easing the pressure on wages even as the working-age population shrank.
3. **Unions chose security over pay.** Unions at large companies prioritised job security, a legacy of the lifetime employment system, over pay rises.
4. **Firms absorbed costs.** Companies squeezed costs through efficiency gains and thinner margins, and practised **shrinkflation**: quietly shrinking pack sizes instead of raising prices.
5. **The government pushed prices down.** Preschool education became free in October 2019, and in 2021 a government campaign forced mobile phone charges down so sharply that it subtracted roughly a percentage point from measured inflation.

The mobile phone episode is worth pausing on. The government pressed the three big carriers to launch cheap plans, and the index of mobile charges fell 38% in a single month, April 2021. Mobile charges carried a weight of about 2.7% in the consumer basket, so a 38% fall knocked about 2.7 × 0.38 ≈ 1 percentage point off the whole index for a year. Fiscal and regulatory policy were working against the central bank's target.

---

## The second tax rise, then the pandemic

In October 2019 the consumption tax finally rose from 8% to 10%, with food kept at 8% and temporary rebates for cashless payments to soften the blow. The economy contracted in the following quarter, helped along by a powerful typhoon.

Then came Covid. Japan relied on voluntary restraint rather than legal lockdowns, but its fiscal response was enormous. The government passed three supplementary budgets in 2020, including a cash handout of **¥100,000 to every resident**, and lent heavily to struggling firms. The BOJ scrapped its bond-purchase guideline in favour of unlimited buying, expanded lending support for companies and raised its ceiling for stock-fund purchases.

Real GDP fell by about 4% in 2020, and gross government debt peaked at about **229% of GDP** on the IMF's current figures. Shinzo Abe stepped down for health reasons in August 2020 after a record tenure; his successors, Yoshihide Suga and Fumio Kishida, kept the broad framework in place.

By the end of 2021 the BOJ owned close to half of all government bonds outstanding, and through its stock-fund purchases it had become the largest single owner of Japanese shares. Its share of JGBs rose from about 11% before QQE to a peak of about 54% in 2023. Notice also the blue line: foreign investors held only a few per cent of JGBs throughout, which is one of the reasons the debt mountain never triggered a crisis.

In March 2021 the BOJ fine-tuned the framework, clarifying that the 10-year yield could move 0.25 percentage points either side of zero and that it would buy stock funds mainly when markets were stressed. Inflation, however, stayed close to zero, and in some months below it.

---

## What it left behind

By the end of 2021 Japan had a central bank that controlled the entire yield curve, a government whose borrowing was in effect being financed by that central bank, and a set of policy settings frozen for a world of zero inflation. Beneath the surface, though, something important had changed: the labour market had quietly tightened, and a generation of flat wages was nearing its end. The question was what would happen if inflation finally arrived. The answer came quickly.

---

## Check yourself

**1. Under yield curve control with a ceiling of 0.25%, the market pushes the 10-year yield up to 0.30%. What does the BOJ do, and what happens to the size of its balance sheet?**

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

It offers to buy unlimited amounts of 10-year bonds at a yield of 0.25% (a fixed-rate operation). Sellers who want out can sell to the BOJ at that price, so the yield is pulled back to the cap. The BOJ pays with newly created reserves, so its **balance sheet grows** by whatever amount it has to buy. The more the market doubts the cap, the bigger the balance sheet gets, which is exactly what happened in 2022.

</details>

**2. A 10-year JGB with a coupon of 0.1% has a modified duration of about 9.9. Roughly how much does its price fall if its yield rises from 0.25% to 0.5%?**

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

Price change ≈ −modified duration × change in yield = −9.9 × 0.25% ≈ **−2.5%**. Small moves in yield mean real money on a large portfolio, which is why each widening of the band mattered to banks and insurers. With a coupon that low, almost all of the bond's value arrives at the end, so its duration is close to its full ten years. (The [bond guide](?slug=global-bond-markets&lesson=lesson-01-anatomy-and-the-seesaw) explains both meanings of duration.)

</details>

**3. If an item with a 2.7% weight in the consumer price index falls in price by 38%, roughly how much does the overall index fall, all else equal?**

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

2.7% × 38% ≈ **1.0 percentage point**. For the twelve months that the cut stays in the year-on-year comparison, measured inflation is about a point lower than it would otherwise be.

</details>

**4. Name three reasons why unemployment of about 2.2% in 2019 did not push Japanese inflation towards 2%.**

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

Any three of: inflation expectations anchored at zero, so firms were afraid to raise prices first; expanding labour supply from women and older workers; unions prioritising job security over pay; firms absorbing costs through efficiency, thinner margins and shrinkflation; and government policies that cut prices directly, such as free preschool and cheaper phone plans.

</details>

---

## What to carry into Lesson 6

- **Yield curve control** targeted the 10-year yield at around zero, defended by unlimited fixed-rate purchases.
- Credibility meant the BOJ could buy *less* for a while: **stealth tapering**.
- A very **tight labour market** still left core inflation at 0.5% to 1%, for reasons of expectations, labour supply, union priorities and government price cuts.
- Covid brought huge fiscal support; debt peaked near **229% of GDP**.
- The BOJ ended up owning about **half the JGB market**.

Lesson 6 is what happened when the world's inflation arrived at Japan's door.
